THOUGHT: Patient is term (38 wks) with sudden severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding after prior cesarean—classic risk for scar dehiscence/rupture. Key features pointing to uterine rupture: prior uterine scar, abrupt severe pain with associated vaginal bleeding, prior contractions that then stopped (loss of uterine tone/contractility), maternal tachycardia and hypotension consistent with intraperitoneal hemorrhage, recurrent variable fetal decelerations indicating fetal compromise, and ultrasound directly showing disruption of uterine wall adjacent to the prior cesarean scar with hemoperitoneum. Differentials like placental abruption typically present with persistent uterine contractions/hypertonus and retroplacental clot rather than free intraperitoneal blood or visible uterine wall discontinuity; vasa previa causes painless bleeding and fetal bradycardia without hemoperitoneum. The imaging plus clinical instability confirm a uterine rupture from the previous scar with intra-abdominal bleeding and fetal distress—an obstetric emergency requiring immediate laparotomy and delivery (and maternal resuscitation).  
DIAGNOSIS: Uterine rupture (complete rupture of the previous cesarean scar with hemoperitoneum).
